title: Fit a cage nut into a rack rail's marked hole: hook one lip from behind, keep the far lip in with a screwdriver
instruction: Fit the cage nut into the marked hole on the rack rail.
context: Racking servers, switches and power units is the hand-done step of data-centre build-out: every device in a square-hole rack is held by screws into cage nuts at its U positions, so each rack takes dozens fitted by hand and an AI data hall thousands. Rack makers give the method: from inside the rack, lips facing out, "Hook one lip of the cage nut in the square rail hole" (Oracle); then "Hold the cage nut in one hand, and compress the cage-nut clip with a flat-blade screwdriver. With the clip compressed, push the edge of the cage nut fully into the hole from the inside of the rack-mounting flange. Release the screwdriver pressure on the clip to lock the cage nut into place." (IBM). One hand holds the hooked nut and turns it home while the other keeps the far clip in line with the hole; turned home alone, that clip's end swings out behind the flange, the nut jams and its hooked clip is levered back out.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x forward, y to the robot's left; heights above the table. A server rack's vertical mounting rail (EIA-310 19-inch, 2 mm steel) stands in a steel foot clamped to the bench, its front (where equipment mounts) facing away from the robot: the mounting flange's back face at x 21.5, the flange from y -3.0 to 0.75 with 9.53 mm square holes centred on y 0, three per U (U lines 2.5 cm above the table and every 4.445 cm above that, numbered 1 to 4 on both faces), and a side flange 3 cm deep along its -y edge. U3's top hole, its middle 15.2 cm above the table, is marked with a yellow paint-pen square. An M6 cage nut (5.5 g: a 10 mm square steel nut, 4.8 mm thick, in a spring-steel cage 10.1 x 11.2 x 6.0 mm, with two 5 mm wide spring lips on opposite sides, 13.72 mm across, for 1.83-2.64 mm panels) lies face down on the bench at (15, 10). A flat-blade screwdriver (40 g; tip 0.6 x 3.5 mm, 60 mm shank, 95 mm handle) lies on the bench along x with its tip at (21.5, -11), pointing toward the robot. The rail is fixed; the nut and the screwdriver are loose. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Poses are read from the simulation and each gripper's centre from the arm's joints. A lip has sprung out over a hole when its end is in front of the flange's front face and 0.2 mm or more past that hole's edge. Score 0 for the rest of the run once: the nut falls onto the bench (after being lifted, its middle below 2 cm with no gripper within 6 cm); a lip springs out at another hole; or a lip is forced 30 degrees or more open (its clip bent). Otherwise 0.5 once the nut sits in the marked hole by itself with at least one lip sprung out over the front face, both grippers' centres 3 cm or more from it and the screwdriver's tip out of the hole (1 cm or more in front of the flange, or 3 cm or more from the nut's middle). 1.0: seated in the marked hole (both lips sprung out over the front face, the nut's axis within 8 degrees of the flange's normal, its face from 1.2 mm behind to 0.5 mm in front of the flange's back face, its middle within 1.5 mm across and 3.5 mm up or down of the hole's middle), released as above and still (moving under 0.5 mm) for 1 s; the trial ends once that has held for another 1 s. On a real rail: both lips out round the marked hole seen from the front, the nut flat against the back, and a light tug does not pull it out.
reset_notes: Press both lips in and take the nut out of the hole; lay it face down at its start and the screwdriver back on the bench, as in the screenshot. Nothing is consumed. In the simulation each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control. The rail, nut, lips and screwdriver are true size. Each spring-steel lip is a rigid folded strip on a sprung hinge at its root (0.02 N m/rad), so it flexes as a whole rather than along its length, with a lighter spring than real spring steel; the nut's M6 thread is not cut (a plain 5 mm bore; only a later screw would use it). The rail is one upright standing in a bench foot rather than a whole rack.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right gripper closed over the screwdriver's handle but never lifted it; the left closed twice beside the rail's foot, then hovered over the cage nut, which never moved from where it lay); demo: 1.0
